claim: Detecting relative rather than absolute changes in extracellular signals enables cells to make decisions in constantly fluctuating environments.
source: Detecting relative rather than absolute changes in extracellular signals enables cells to make decisions in constantly fluctuating environments.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular signaling that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Mammalian cells use a novel non-transcriptional mechanism of relative sensing based on receptor abundance.
source: Using the growth factor-activated PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, we develop here computational and analytical models, and experimentally validate a novel non-transcriptional mechanism of relative sensing in mammalian cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents computational models and experimental validation of this mechanism.

claim: Cells encode past stimulation levels in the abundance of cognate receptors on the cell surface.
source: This mechanism relies on a new form of cellular memory, where cells effectively encode past stimulation levels in the abundance of cognate receptors on the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of surface receptor abundance at different background stimulation levels.

claim: Surface receptor abundance is regulated by background signal-dependent receptor endocytosis and down-regulation.
source: The surface receptor abundance is regulated by background signal-dependent receptor endocytosis and down-regulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing receptor abundance changes with background stimulation.

claim: Relative sensing is robust and specific for EGF and HGF across wide ranges of background stimuli.
source: We show the robustness and specificity of relative sensing for two physiologically important ligands, epidermal growth factor (EGF) and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and across wide ranges of background stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with both ligands at multiple background concentrations.

claim: E. coli chemotaxis is a classic example of relative sensing in bacteria.
source: Relative sensing of environmental inputs has been previosuly investigated in bacteria, with the E. coli chemotaxis being a classic example (Mesibov et al., 1973; Barkai and Leibler, 1997; Alon et al., 1999; Shoval et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on bacterial chemotaxis.

claim: Fold changes in ERK nuclear activity were robust to cell-to-cell variability when responding to constant stimuli.
source: When responding to constant stimuli, experiments with the signaling proteins ERK (Cohen-Saidon et al., 2009) and β-catenin (Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009) showed that fold changes in their nuclear activity were robust to cell-to-cell variability (Cohen-Saidon et al., 2009) and variability in signaling network parameters (Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on ERK signaling.

claim: Genes directly controlled by NF-κB often respond to its fold changes at the single cell level.
source: Later studies of the NF-κB (Lee et al., 2014) and TGF-β/SMAD pathways (Frick et al., 2017) also showed that genes directly controlled by these proteins often respond to their fold changes at the single cell level.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on NF-κB signaling.

claim: Chlorophyll activity in plants was found to be proportional to the fold change in external light intensity.
source: Recent work has explored relative sensing at the organism level in plants, where the chlorophyll activity was found to be proportional to the fold change in external light intensity (Tendler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on plant light sensing.

claim: Akt serves as a central hub of multiple growth factor-activated signaling cascades.
source: Akt serves as a central hub of multiple growth factor-activated signaling cascades (Hemmings and Restuccia, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on Akt signaling.

claim: Akt phosphorylation-dependent pathways are implicated in multiple human diseases including cancers, diabetes, and psychiatric disorders.
source: Naturally, Akt phosphorylation-dependent (pAkt) pathways are implicated in multiple human diseases, such as many types of cancers (Engelman, 2009; Hemmings and Restuccia, 2012), diabetes (Whiteman et al., 2002), and psychiatric disorders (Gilman et al., 2012; McGuire et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on disease associations.

claim: Within minutes of continuous EGF stimulation, pAkt reached maximum response and then decayed to low steady state levels within hours.
source: Within minutes of continuous stimulation with EGF pAkt reached maximum response, and then decayed to low steady state levels within hours (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental time course data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Steady state pAkt levels were approximately independent of the EGF stimulus, indicating an approximately adaptive response.
source: The resulting steady state pAkt levels were approximately independent of the EGF stimulus, indicating an approximately adaptive response (Friedlander and Brenner, 2009; Shoval et al., 2010; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to adaptation literature.

claim: Maximal pAkt response was approximately proportional to the logarithm of the EGF stimulus in the sensitive range of EGF concentrations.
source: In the sensitive range of EGF concentrations, maximal pAkt response was approximately proportional to the logarithm of the EGF stimulus (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: pAkt levels were approximately linearly proportional to the phosphorylation level of EGF receptors in the logarithmic regime.
source: Quantitative western blot experiments demonstrated that in this logarithmic regime, pAkt levels were approximately linearly proportional to the phosphorylation level of EGF receptors (EGFRs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The logarithmic dependence of EGFR phosphorylation levels on EGF stimulation has been previously attributed to a mixture of receptor species with varying affinities, negative cooperativity, and oligomeric aggregation.
source: The logarithmic dependence of EGFR phosphorylation levels on EGF stimulation has been previously attributed to a mixture of receptor species with varying affinities to the ligand, negative cooperativity of ligand binding to receptor dimers, and oligomeric aggregation of receptors (Kawamoto et al., 1983; Chatelier et al., 1986; Wofsy et al., 1992; Macdonald and Pike, 2008; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on EGFR binding properties.

claim: Continuous stimulation with EGF resulted in the abundance of cell-surface EGF receptors decreasing proportionally to the logarithm of the background EGF level.
source: Continuous stimulation with EGF resulted in the abundance of cell-surface EGF receptors (sEGFR) also decreasing proportionally to the logarithm of the background EGF level, and reaching a new steady state within hours (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on surface EGFR levels shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Prior exposure with EGF desensitized cells to subsequent EGF stimulations in a quantitative manner.
source: Notably, prior exposure with EGF desensitized cells to subsequent EGF stimulations in a quantitative manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced pAkt response after pre-exposure.

claim: When cells were pre-exposed to different levels of EGF for 3 hr and then stimulated with the same final EGF concentration (2 ng/ml), the maximal pAkt response decreased monotonically with increasing pre-exposure EGF levels.
source: When we first pre-exposed cells to different levels of EGF for 3 hr and then stimulated them with the same final EGF concentration (2 ng/ml)), the maximal pAkt response decreased monotonically with increasing pre-exposure EGF levels (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The pAkt response to an abrupt EGF stimulation is strongly affected by background EGF levels, likely mediated by endocytosis-based removal of activated EGFRs from the cell surface.
source: These experiments demonstrate that the pAkt response to an abrupt EGF stimulation is strongly affected by background EGF levels, and that this effect is likely mediated by the endocytosis-based removal of activated EGFRs from the cell surface (Wiley et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work on receptor endocytosis.

claim: The desensitization of the phosphorylation response was likely due to receptor-based mechanisms upstream of Akt activation.
source: Using pharmacological perturbations of the EGFR/Akt pathway, we confirmed that the desensitization of the phosphorylation response (Figure 1d) was likely due to receptor-based mechanisms upstream of Akt activation, and did not depend on its downregulation, for example, through phosphorylation-dependent Akt degradation (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological perturbation experiments with SC79 and citation to previous work.

claim: SC79 is a small molecule which promotes Akt phosphorylation even in the absence of extracellular ligands.
source: Specifically, we used SC79, a small molecule which promotes Akt phosphorylation even in the absence of extracellular ligands (Jo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on SC79.

claim: The pAkt response following stimulation with SC79 did not depend on the background EGF pre-exposure.
source: Unlike the desensitization observed in the growth factor-induced pAkt response (Figure 1d), the pAkt response following stimulation with SC79 did not depend on the background EGF pre-exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The EGF desensitization mechanism was upstream of Akt.
source: This result supports the conclusion that the EGF desensitization mechanism was upstream of Akt.
evidence: This is inferred from the SC79 experimental results.

claim: The ODE model included endocytosis and degradation of activated receptors.
source: The model included several well-established features of the EGFR signaling cascade (Chen et al., 2009), such as endocytosis and degradation of activated receptors (Materials and methods) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is described in the model construction and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The model predicted that the maximal pAkt response depends primarily on the EGF fold change relative to the background stimulation levels.
source: The model predicted that the maximal pAkt response indeed depends primarily on the EGF fold change relative to the background stimulation levels (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by computational model predictions shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Relative sensing of EGF stimuli occurred over an order of magnitude of background EGF concentrations.
source: This relative sensing of EGF stimuli occurred over an order of magnitude of background EGF concentrations, and the resulting pAkt response was approximately proportional to the logarithm of the EGF fold change (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by computational model predictions shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The model predicted relative sensing exactly in the range of EGF background concentrations where sEGFR endocytosis was sensitive to background ligand stimulation.
source: Notably, the model predicted relative sensing exactly in the range of EGF background concentrations where sEGFR endocytosis was sensitive to background ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the computational model analysis.

claim: At low EGF background concentrations (<0.01 ng/ml), no substantial sEGFR removal was predicted at the steady state.
source: At low EGF background concentrations (<0.01 ng/ml), no substantial sEGFR removal was predicted at the steady state (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and consequently there was no significant desensitization of the pAkt response.
evidence: This is supported by computational model predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At high background EGF concentrations (>1 ng/ml), a large fraction of sEGFR was already removed from cell surface and the network responded only weakly to further EGF stimulation.
source: In contrast, at high background EGF concentrations (>1 ng/ml), a large fraction of sEGFR was already removed from cell surface and consequently the network responded only weakly to further EGF stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the computational model analysis.

claim: Experiments confirmed that maximal pAkt response depends primarily on the fold change of EGF and not its absolute concentration across more than an order of magnitude of EGF background concentrations (0.03–0.5 ng/ml).
source: Similar results were observed in two independent biological replicates (Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3), and the experiments confirmed the predictions of the computational model that maximal pAkt response depends primarily on the fold change of EGF and not its absolute concentration (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 4). Specifically, across more than an order of magnitude of EGF background concentrations (0.03–0.5 ng/ml) the same EGF fold change (lines with the same colors in Figure 3a) elicited similar pAkt responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and supplementary figures.

claim: The concentration range in which relative sensing was observed was consistent with recent estimations of in vivo EGF levels.
source: The concentration range in which we obsered relative sensing was consistent with recent estimations of in vivo EGF levels (Pinilla-Macua et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on in vivo EGF levels.

claim: The maximal pAkt response was approximately proportional to the logarithm of EGF fold change.
source: In close agreement with the computational model predictions, the maximal pAkt response was approximately proportional to the logarithm of EGF fold change (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Approximate relative sensing was also observed for the time integral of pAkt levels.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the maximal pAkt response, approximate relative sensing was also observed for the time integral of pAkt levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), and for the entire time course of pAkt dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: An increase in the value of α increases signal sensitivity and receptor dimerization and phosphorylation, shifting the relative sensing range to lower ligand concentrations.
source: Notably, an increase in the value of α increases signal sensitivity and receptor dimerization and phosphorylation. This shifts the relative sensing range to lower ligand concentrations (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by analytical model predictions shown in Figure 5a.

claim: An increase in the value of β increases the fraction of active receptors being internalized and degraded, increasing the range of background ligand concentrations where relative sensing is observed.
source: In turn, an increase in the value of β increases the fraction of active receptors being internalized and degraded. This increases the range of background ligand concentrations where the relative sensing is observed (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by analytical model predictions shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Based on the best-fit ODE model parameter sets, α is estimated to be approximately 15 and β is estimated to be approximately 40.
source: Based on the best-fit ODE model parameter sets, we estimate α ~ 15 and β ~ 40 (Appendix).
evidence: This is derived from fitting the ODE model to experimental data.

claim: The relative sensing occurs across over an order of magnitude of background ligand concentrations.
source: The model analysis showed that the relative sensing occurs across over an order of magnitude of background ligand concentrations (Appendix).
evidence: This is derived from the analytical model analysis.

claim: Relative sensing does not require receptor dimerization, and similar sensing mechanisms can operate in pathways where signaling is initiated by monomeric receptors.
source: Furthermore, the analytical model revealed that relative sensing does not require receptor dimerization, and similar sensing mechanisms can operate in pathways where signaling is initiated by monomeric receptors (Appendix).
evidence: This is derived from the analytical model analysis.

claim: Akt phosphorylation can be induced by multiple ligands including hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) which binds to its cognate receptor cMet.
source: In addition to EGF, Akt phosphorylation can be induced by multiple other ligands, including hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) (Stuart et al., 2000) which binds to its cognate receptor cMet (Viticchiè and Muller, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on HGF/cMet signaling.

claim: Upon ligand binding, cMet receptors dimerize and cross-phosphorylate each other, leading to phosphorylation of multiple downstream targets including Akt.
source: Similar to EGFRs, upon ligand binding, cMet receptors dimerize (Kong-Beltran et al., 2004) and cross-phosphorylate each other; this leads to phosphorylation of multiple downstream targets, including Akt.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on cMet receptor activation.

claim: Pre-exposure with HGF did not substantially downregulate EGF-induced pAkt responses, but substantially decreased HGF-induced responses.
source: Pre-exposure with HGF did not substantially downregulate EGF-induced pAkt responses, but substantially decreased HGF-induced responses (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There was a relatively small desensitization of HGF-induced responses due to pre-exposure with EGF, while there was a significant desensitization of EGF-induced pAkt responses.
source: Similarly, we observed a relatively small desensitization of HGF-induced responses due to pre-exposure with EGF, while there was a significant desensitization of EGF-induced pAkt responses (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Exposure of MCF10A cells to various concentrations of HGF leads to pronounced HGF-dependent removal of cMet from the cell surface, without significant removal of sEGFR.
source: We further confirmed that exposure of MCF10A cells to various concentrations of HGF leads to pronounced HGF-dependent removal of cMet from the cell surface, without significant removal of sEGFR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-exposure of cells to EGF leads to EGF-dependent removal of sEGFR without a significant change in surface cMet abundance.
source: Similarly, the pre-exposure of cells to EGF leads to EGF-dependent removal of sEGFR without a significant change in surface cMet abundance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relative sensing of extracellular ligands relies on the memory of their past exposures effectively encoded in the abundances of their cognate cell-surface receptors.
source: These observations support the mechanism in which the relative sensing of extracellular ligands relies on the memory of their past exposures effectively encoded in the abundances of their cognate cell-surface receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the ligand-specific desensitization experiments.

claim: HGF-induced phosphorylation of Akt depends primarily on the fold change in extracellular HGF concentration across almost an order of magnitude of background HGF exposures (between 0.1 and 1 ng/ml HGF).
source: These experiments demonstrated that HGF-induced phosphorylation of Akt also depends primarily on the fold change in extracellular HGF concentration across almost an order of magnitude of background HGF exposures (between 0.1 and 1 ng/ml HGF) (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The maximum pAkt levels depended approximately log-linearly on the HGF fold change.
source: Moreover, like EGF, the maximum pAkt levels depended approximately log-linearly on the HGF fold change (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: FoxO3 transcription factor is a key effector of the PI3K-Akt pathway, involved in diverse cellular processes including apoptosis, proliferation, and metabolism.
source: The FoxO3 transcription factor is a key effector of the pathway, and it is involved in diverse cellular processes including apoptosis, proliferation, and metabolism (Webb and Brunet, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on FoxO3.

claim: Akt phosphorylation of FoxO3 leads to its translocation from the nucleus to cytoplasm and subsequent transcriptional deactivation.
source: Akt phosphorylation of FoxO3 leads to its translocation from the nucleus to cytoplasm and subsequent transcriptional deactivation (Webb and Brunet, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on FoxO3 regulation.

claim: Following Akt activation, the typical nuclear translocation timescale for FoxO family proteins is short (less than 5 min).
source: Notably, following Akt activation, the typical nuclear translocation timescale for FoxO family proteins is short (less than 5 min) (Gross and Rotwein, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on FoxO translocation kinetics.

claim: The nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio of FoxO3 reflected the relative, rather than the absolute changes in EGF stimulation.
source: Consistent with relative sensing by pAkt, the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio of FoxO3 also reflected the relative, rather than the absolute changes in EGF stimulation (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Relative sensing of the growth factor signal is faithfully transmitted in MCF10A cells to at least some of the physiologically important effectors of the PI3K-Akt pathway.
source: Thus, relative sensing of the growth factor signal is faithfully transmitted in MCF10A cells to at least some of the physiologically important effectors of the PI3K-Akt pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the FoxO3 experimental results.

claim: Receptor endocytosis may allow cells to continuously monitor signals in their environment by dynamically adjusting the number of ligand-cognate receptors on the cell surface.
source: Specifically, receptor endocytosis may allow cells to continuously monitor signals in their environment (Becker et al., 2010; Brennan et al., 2012; Mitchell et al., 2015) by dynamically adjusting the number of ligand-cognate receptors on the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and the current study's findings.

claim: The memory of past stimuli, effectively encoded in the number of surface receptors, may be signal-specific, at least for some ligands, due to the selective removal of ligand-cognate receptors.
source: Our analysis also demonstrates that the memory of past stimuli, effectively encoded in the number of surface receptors, may be signal-specific, at least for some ligands, due to the selective removal of ligand-cognate receptors.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data on ligand-specific desensitization.

claim: The combination of logarithmic pAkt response and the logarithmic dependence of the ligand-specific memory on the background signal allows cells to respond to relative changes in environmental stimuli.
source: The combination of logarithmic pAkt response, and the logarithmic dependence of the ligand-specific memory on the background signal, allows cells to respond to relative changes in environmental stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental and modeling results.

claim: The described relative sensing mechanism is not a direct consequence of either simple adaptation to various levels of background signals or logarithmic activation response.
source: We note that the described relative sensing mechanism is not a direct consequence of either simple adaptation to various levels of background signals or logarithmic activation response (Shoval et al., 2010; Adler et al., 2017; Adler and Alon, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a clarification with citations to previous work on adaptation and logarithmic responses.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that transcriptional motifs may efficiently buffer cell-to-cell variability in signaling components when responding to a constant extracellular stimulation.
source: Previous studies (Cohen-Saidon et al., 2009; Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009; Lee et al., 2014) have demonstrated that transcriptional motifs may efficiently buffer cell-to-cell variability in signaling components when responding to a constant extracellular stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on transcriptional buffering.

claim: The study describes a non-transcriptional mechanism of sensing extracellular signal changes relative to past extracellular stimulation.
source: In contrast, our study describes a non-transcriptional mechanism of sensing extracellular signal changes relative to past extracellular stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to previous transcriptional mechanisms.

claim: The pAkt response to an abrupt stimulation is relatively fast (~5–15 min) and therefore non-transcriptional in nature.
source: Although the pAkt response to an abrupt stimulation is relatively fast (~5–15 min, Figure 1a), and therefore non-transcriptional in nature, the sustained production and delivery of cell surface receptors is essential to establishing the signal-dependent and receptor-mediated memory.
evidence: This is supported by the time course data in Figure 1a.

claim: Sustained transcription and translation of network components are necessary for proper functioning of the described sensing mechanism.
source: Therefore, sustained transcription and translation of network comonents are necessary for proper functioning of the described sensing mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for receptor production and delivery.

claim: There are usually ~10^5–10^6 EGFR receptors on mammalian cell surface.
source: Although there are usually ~105–106 EGFR receptors on mammalian cell surface (Shi et al., 2016), the downstream network response, for example Akt phosphorylation, often saturates when only a relatively small fraction (5–10%) of the receptors are bound to their cognate ligands (Chen et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on receptor abundance.

claim: The downstream network response often saturates when only a relatively small fraction (5–10%) of the receptors are bound to their cognate ligands.
source: Although there are usually ~105–106 EGFR receptors on mammalian cell surface (Shi et al., 2016), the downstream network response, for example Akt phosphorylation, often saturates when only a relatively small fraction (5–10%) of the receptors are bound to their cognate ligands (Chen et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on receptor saturation.

claim: One potential advantage of having excess receptors is that it may endow cells with a large dynamic range of receptor abundances to memorize stimulation levels of multiple extracellular ligands.
source: Our study suggests that one potential advantage of such a system architecture is that, beyond simple signal activation, it may endow cells with a large dynamic range of receptor abundances to memorize stimulation levels of multiple extracellular ligands (Hart et al., 2013; Nandagopal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Signal-mediated removal has been reported for many other receptors and signaling systems, such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and AMPA-type glutamate receptors.
source: Notably, signal-mediated removal has been reported for many other receptors and signaling systems, such as the G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Ferguson, 2001), involved in various sensory systems, and AMPA-type glutamate receptors (Guskjolen, 2016), implicated in synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on receptor removal in other systems.

claim: Similar relative sensing mechanisms may be important in multiple other receptor-based signaling cascades and across different biological contexts.
source: Therefore, similar relative sensing mechanisms may be important in multiple other receptor-based signaling cascades and across different biological contexts.
evidence: This is speculated based on the prevalence of signal-mediated receptor removal in other systems.

claim: MCF10A cells were obtained from the ATCC and grown according to ATCC recommendations.
source: MCF10A cells were obtained from the ATCC and grown according to ATCC recommendations.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell source and culture.

claim: Cell identity was confirmed by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
source: Cell identity was confirmed by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and cells were tested with the MycoAlert PLUS mycoplasma detection kit (Lonza) and found to be free of Mycoplasma prior to analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell authentication.

claim: Cells were tested and found to be free of Mycoplasma prior to analyses.
source: Cell identity was confirmed by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and cells were tested with the MycoAlert PLUS mycoplasma detection kit (Lonza) and found to be free of Mycoplasma prior to analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about contamination testing.

claim: The rates of internalization, recycling, and degradation are different for inactive (unphosphorylated) and active (phosphorylated) receptors.
source: In agreement with available literature (Wiley and Cunningham, 1982; Herbst et al., 1994), we assumed that the rates of internalization, recycling, and degradation are different for inactive (unphosphorylated) and active (phosphorylated) receptors (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EGFR phosphatases in MCF10A cells are present at exceedingly high concentrations.
source: We assumed that EGFR phosphatases in MCF10A cells are present at exceedingly high concentrations (Kleiman et al., 2011), and therefore we implemented the corresponding reaction of dephosphorylation of phosphorylated EGFRs (pEGFRs) as a first order reaction.
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Activated receptors on plasma membrane and in endosomes are dephosphorylated by the phosphatase with the same rate.
source: We further assumed that activated receptors on plasma membrane and in endosomes are dephosphorylated by the phosphatase with the same rate (Kleiman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Akt can be phosphorylated only by cell-surface pEGFR, and not by endosomal pEGFR.
source: In agreement with the literature (Haugh and Meyer, 2002; Park et al., 2003), we assumed that Akt can be phosphorylated only by cell-surface pEGFR, and not by endosomal pEGFR.
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citations to previous literature.
